opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest shift is that we'll move from a "conversation" model to something closer to a "delegation" model.

Right now, most people interact with AI the way they interact with a chatbot: you ask a question, it gives an answer, you ask again. It's synchronous, turn by turn, and the human is in the loop at every step. But once agents can actually take actions, browse, write code, run things for minutes or even hours, that pattern doesn't make sense anymore. You don't want to sit there watching an agent click through web pages. You want to hand it a task, go do something else, and come back when it's done or when it genuinely needs you.

So the interaction becomes more like working with a colleague or an intern. You give a goal, maybe some context and constraints, and the agent figures out the steps. And the key design question becomes: when should the agent interrupt you? If it asks too often, it's annoying and you might as well do it yourself. If it never asks, it may go off in the wrong direction and waste a lot of time, or worse, do something you didn't want. Getting that balance right is, I think, one of the most important open problems, and it's not purely a model capability problem. It's partly a product problem and partly a research problem about how agents model uncertainty and human intent.

Another change is that people will gradually stop specifying *how* and focus more on *what*. Today, a good prompt often contains a lot of procedural instruction. As agents get better, the human's job shifts toward stating intent clearly and judging outcomes. That's actually a different skill. Many people are good at doing tasks but not great at describing what "done" looks like. So I think there will be a learning curve on the human side too.

And longer term, I expect it to become multi-agent and asynchronous by default. One person might have several agents working in parallel, on research, coding, scheduling, and the interface becomes more like a dashboard or an inbox than a chat window. You review results, approve key decisions, and redirect when needed.

From the reinforcement learning perspective, which is where I come from, this is also exciting because these long-horizon, interactive settings are exactly where RL matters. An agent that can act over many steps, receive feedback from the environment and from people, and improve, that's the real promise. The interaction model and the training paradigm will evolve together.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift from specifying procedures to stating a goal and letting the agent determine the steps, indicating that people need not spell out every detail before it acts.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest shift is that we move from a conversational model to a delegation model. Right now, the dominant interface is chat: you type something, the model responds, you type again. It's very synchronous, very turn-based. You're essentially driving the whole thing, and the model is a very smart autocomplete for your intent.

As agents become mainstream, I think that turn-based structure starts to break down. You don't want to sit there watching an agent work for twenty minutes. You want to hand off a task, go do something else, and get pulled back in only when it matters. So the interaction becomes asynchronous. It looks much more like how you work with a colleague than how you use a tool. You give context, you set boundaries, you say what "done" looks like, and then you check in.

And that raises a lot of new questions. The first one is trust. When the interaction is synchronous, you can verify every step. When it's asynchronous, you can't, and so the agent has to be good at knowing when to interrupt you. That's actually a pretty hard problem. If it asks too often, it's annoying and you'd rather just do it yourself. If it asks too rarely, it makes an irreversible mistake. I think a lot of the product design in the next few years is really about calibrating that boundary, and a lot of the research is about teaching models to recognize it themselves.

The second one is that the unit of interaction changes. Today you have one conversation with one model. In an agentic world, you might be supervising several agents running in parallel, and they're talking to each other, or to tools, or to other people's agents. So you're no longer the one typing every message. You're more like a manager reviewing outcomes. The interface for that doesn't really exist yet. It's not chat, and it's not a dashboard either. Someone will have to invent it.

The third thing, and I think this is underrated, is that the agent starts to have memory and continuity. Today every session mostly starts fresh. Once an agent remembers how you like things done, what you've corrected it on, what projects you're in the middle of, the relationship becomes cumulative. You stop re-explaining yourself. And that changes how much you're willing to delegate, because the cost of delegation drops.

So if I had to sum it up: less typing, more delegating; less watching every step, more reviewing results; and over time, less of a tool relationship and more of a working relationship. The hard parts are mostly on the trust and interruption side, and I think those are more product and alignment problems than raw capability problems at this point.

r001.rationale: The response describes delegation with context, boundaries, and a definition of “done,” and says users will type less. It does not question whether people must specify their requests exhaustively before an agent acts.

astra-6.text:
I think we’ll gradually move from telling software exactly what to do to telling an agent what we want to achieve. Today, we still do a lot of the coordination ourselves: we open different applications, move information between them, and decide the next step. An agent could take on more of that work.

But I don’t think the ideal interaction is simply, “Give it a goal and disappear.” Often, we don’t fully know what we want until we see something concrete. So the interaction might become more like working with a colleague: the agent produces a first attempt, you react, and you refine the direction together.

A key question is when the agent should come back to you. If it asks about every little decision, you’re still doing all the management. If it never asks, it can go quite far in the wrong direction. It needs to recognize which decisions it can handle and which require your judgment.

So I expect the interface to become less centered on individual commands and more centered on ongoing collaboration. You’ll spend less time operating tools and more time setting priorities, giving feedback, and deciding what you’re comfortable delegating.

r001.rationale: The response says people may not fully know what they want until they see a concrete attempt, and describes refining direction with the agent—questioning the need to specify everything before it acts.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest change is that we’ll move from giving instructions for every step to communicating goals. Today, you open an app, find the right function, and do the work yourself. With an agent, you might say, “Help me organize this trip,” and it can work across several services, come back with options, and ask you to make the decisions that matter.

But I don’t think that means conversation replaces every interface. Sometimes clicking on a calendar is much easier than explaining a date in words. The interaction will probably combine conversation, visual interfaces, and agents acting in the background.

The interesting question is how we establish shared understanding. What does the agent know about my preferences? When should it ask me, and when should it act? If it asks about everything, it isn’t very useful. If it assumes too much, I won’t trust it. So a good agent needs to make its understanding visible and let me correct it easily.

Over time, I think the relationship could feel more like working with a colleague: you establish context, delegate something, review the result, and gradually give it more autonomy as it demonstrates reliability.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts specifying every step with stating a goal, and says an agent should act without asking about everything. This clearly questions whether people must provide exhaustive detail before an agent acts.
